Queue::invoke¶

Back to Queue API Reference

Signature¶

Queue invoke(std::string_view method, std::span<const Arg> args = {}) const;
Queue invoke(std::string_view method, std::initializer_list<Arg> args) const;
Queue invoke(std::initializer_list<std::string_view> methods) const;

What It Does¶

invoke calls a method by name on the held payload – Series, Note, Timeline, or Duration – the same way you would call it directly on that type, but through a name string instead of a member-function call. This is the general-purpose way to reach a method generically, without first branching on kind() and calling the matching accessor.

Timeline also accepts a handful of friendlier names – "year", "month", "day", "hour", "minute", "second", "quarter", "weekday", "dayofyear", "week" – which are translated to Timeline’s own registered method names before the call (so "year" reaches the same method Timeline::year() calls directly). Any other method name passes through unchanged. If a Timeline method isn’t found under the (possibly translated) name, two fallbacks are tried: a Series-flavored lookup, then a Note-flavored one, since some Timeline operations are implemented alongside those types. Duration looks a method up directly, with the same two fallbacks on a miss.

Each argument converts implicitly – an integer, a floating-point number, a boolean, a string, a list of integers, or a Series/Note/Timeline/ Duration value can all be written directly in the argument list ({2.0}, {"some text"}) with no explicit wrapping needed, the same way Queue’s own constructors are implicit.

Three overloads exist: a single method with a list of arguments (spelled either as a span or a braced initializer_list – both accept {2.0} directly), and a third overload that takes a list of method names rather than arguments, applying each one in turn, with no arguments to any of them, to the result of the last.

Parameters¶

method (std::string_view)

The method name to call, in the payload’s own naming convention (or one of the handful of Timeline aliases above).

args (a list of arguments, default empty)

The arguments to pass. Each one converts implicitly from an integer, floating-point number, boolean, string, list of integers, or a Series/Note/Timeline/Duration value.

methods (a list of method names, three-argument-less overload only)

A sequence of method names, each applied with no arguments to the result of the previous call, left to right. An empty method name anywhere in the list is refused.

Returns¶

A new Queue wrapping whatever the called method returned, re-wrapped by kind the same way the original constructors are.

Errors¶

Throws when the payload doesn’t have a method by that name (after any Timeline alias translation and fallback attempts), or when an argument of a type the method doesn’t accept is passed. The chained, method-names-only overload also throws if any name in the list is empty.

invoke also cannot reach an in-place, trailing-underscore method (Series’s add_, mul_, and the rest) by name – it always throws, regardless of the payload’s kind. Mutating a Queue’s held value is only possible through the non-const accessor, calling the in-place method directly: q.series().add_(x), not q.invoke("add_", {x}).

Examples¶

Example 1. invoke("mul", ...) on a Series-holding Queue – the argument converts implicitly, with no explicit wrapping.

pluss::Queue series_q(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}));
pluss::Queue doubled = series_q.invoke("mul", {2.0});
std::cout << "series invoke(mul, 2.0): " << pluss::series::print(doubled.series()) << '\n';

Output¶

series invoke(mul, 2.0): Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2.0000, 4.0000, 6.0000]

Example 2. invoke("upper") on a Note-holding Queue.

pluss::Queue note_q(pluss::make_note({"ab", "cd"}));
pluss::Queue note_upper = note_q.invoke("upper");
std::cout << "note invoke(upper): " << note_upper.note() << '\n';

Output¶

note invoke(upper): Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=utf8)
["AB", "CD"]

Example 3. invoke("year") on a Timeline-holding Queue – "year" is translated to the name Timeline::year() is registered under before the call.

pluss::Queue timeline_q(pluss::timeline::make("1999-04-17T21:15:23Z"));
pluss::Queue year_q = timeline_q.invoke("year");
std::cout << "timeline invoke(year): "
          << pluss::series::print(year_q.series()) << '\n';

Output¶

timeline invoke(year): Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=int32, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=1999

The result comes back as a plain Series wrapped in a Queue – Timeline::year() returns a Series, not another Timeline, so the returned Queue’s kind() is Series, not Timeline.

Example 4. The chained, method-names-only overload: neg then abs, applied in sequence to a Series-holding Queue, with no arguments to either.

pluss::Queue series_q(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}));
pluss::Queue chained = series_q.invoke({"neg", "abs"});
std::cout << "chained invoke({neg, abs}): " << pluss::series::print(chained.series()) << '\n';

Output¶

chained invoke({neg, abs}): Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000, 2.0000, 3.0000]

Negating then taking the absolute value returns the original magnitudes – neg followed by abs is a round trip for any already-positive input.

Example 5. invoke cannot reach an in-place method – "add_" throws, even though Series::add_ itself is a perfectly real method.

pluss::Queue series_q(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}));
try {
  pluss::Queue bad = series_q.invoke("add_", {1.0});
  std::cout << "invoke(add_): did not throw\n";
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << "invoke(add_) threw: " << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n')) << '\n';
}

Output¶

invoke(add_) threw: Unrouted op on CPU (strict mode): add_(double) has no route to a kernel; it would otherwise return the receiver unchanged (a silent identity). Implement it or remove the call.

To mutate the Series a Queue holds, call add_ directly off the non-const accessor instead – series_q.series().add_(x) – which is real C++ method dispatch, not a name string, so it reaches add_ without going through invoke at all. See accessors’s Example 2.

See Also¶

  • operators: +, -, *, and the comparison operators are themselves thin wrappers around invoke for Series, Timeline, and Duration payloads.

  • where: the one operation Queue exposes as a static method rather than through invoke.
